title: Moving Data: mov, lea and Addressing Modes
summary: Most instructions in real code just move data: between registers, from memory into a register, from a register back to memory. This lesson covers `mov` and its widening relatives `movzx` and `movsx`, the **addressing modes** that let one instruction compute an address like `base + index × scale + offset`, and `lea`, which does that arithmetic without touching memory at all.
markdown:
## mov

`mov destination, source` copies a value. It never changes the source and never sets the flags.

```asm
mov   eax, 10                  ; constant into a register
mov   ecx, eax                 ; register to register
mov   eax, dword ptr [rcx]     ; 4 bytes from memory at the address in rcx, into eax
mov   qword ptr [rsp+20h], rax ; 8 bytes from rax into memory at rsp+0x20
mov   byte ptr [rdx], 1        ; the constant 1 into one byte of memory
```

The **size** comes from the register (`eax` is 4 bytes, `rax` 8). When there is no register to tell it (a constant stored to memory), the size is written out: `byte ptr`, `word ptr` (2), `dword ptr` (4), `qword ptr` (8). Disassemblers show the `ptr` sizes on every memory operand, which is a gift when reading code: `dword ptr [rcx+8]` tells you there is a 4-byte value 8 bytes into whatever `rcx` points at.

## Widening: movzx and movsx

Loading a 1-byte `char` or 2-byte `short` into a 32-bit register needs to fill the extra bits, and how depends on whether the type is signed:

| Instruction | Fills the new upper bits with | For |
|---|---|---|
| `movzx eax, byte ptr [rcx]` | Zeros (**zero extension**) | `unsigned char`, `bool`, `std::uint16_t` |
| `movsx eax, byte ptr [rcx]` | Copies of the sign bit (**sign extension**) | `signed char`, `short` |
| `movsxd rax, ecx` | Sign extension from 32 to 64 bits | `int` to `long long` or to an index |

The byte `0xFF` becomes 255 with `movzx` and -1 with `movsx`. This is two's complement from lesson 1.02, done by hardware.

## Addressing modes

A memory operand can compute its address from up to four parts:

```
[ base + index × scale + displacement ]
   reg    reg    1,2,4,8   constant
```

| Form | Typical C++ |
|---|---|
| `[rcx]` | `*p` |
| `[rcx+8]` | `p->member` at offset 8 (lesson 2.06) |
| `[rcx+rdx*4]` | `array[i]` for 4-byte elements: base address `rcx`, index `rdx` |
| `[rcx+rdx*8+10h]` | `p->items[i]` where `items` is an array of 8-byte values at offset 0x10 |
| `[rip+1234h]` | A global variable, relative to the instruction (lesson 6.09) |

The scale can only be 1, 2, 4 or 8: exactly the sizes of `char`, `short`, `int`/`float` and pointers/`double`. Indexing arrays of those types costs no extra instructions at all.

Step through a loop that sums an array. `rdi` holds the array's address; `[rdi+rcx*4]` is `values[i]`:

```demo-asm
title: Summing int values[4] through [rdi+rcx*4]
init: rdi=0x2000, mem@0x2000=10 20 30 40
    xor  eax, eax
    xor  ecx, ecx
next:
    add  eax, dword ptr [rdi+rcx*4]
    inc  ecx
    cmp  ecx, 4
    jl   next
    ret
```

## lea: the address calculator

`lea` ("load effective address") computes the address of a memory operand and puts the **address itself** into the destination, without reading memory:

```asm
lea   rax, [rcx+rdx*4]      ; rax = rcx + rdx*4         (&array[i])
lea   rax, [rcx+10h]        ; rax = rcx + 16            (&p->member)
lea   rcx, [rip+1F2Ah]      ; rcx = the address of a global or string literal
```

Because the address hardware can add two registers, scale one of them and add a constant in a single step, compilers also use `lea` for plain arithmetic that has nothing to do with addresses:

| C++ | Compiled |
|---|---|
| `x + 50` (into a different register) | `lea eax, [rcx+32h]` (lesson 1.04's example) |
| `a + b` | `lea eax, [rcx+rdx]` |
| `x * 5` | `lea eax, [rcx+rcx*4]` |
| `x * 9 + 3` | `lea eax, [rcx+rcx*8+3]` |

When you see `lea` in compiler output, ask whether it is computing a pointer or just doing quick arithmetic. Both are common.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Confusing `mov rax, [rcx]` with `lea rax, [rcx]`
> `mov` reads the 8 bytes at the address; `lea` puts the address itself in `rax`. One is `*p`, the other is `p`.

> [!warning] Reading `[rcx+rdx*4]` as "rcx plus rdx plus 4"
> The `*4` scales the index: it is element `rdx` of an array of 4-byte values.

> [!warning] Assuming `mov` sets flags
> It does not. A comparison needs `cmp` or `test`.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What four parts can a memory operand's address have?
+ A base register, an index register multiplied by 1, 2, 4 or 8, and a constant displacement
- A segment, a page number, an offset and a size
- Two registers added together, a multiplier of any value, and a variable name
- A base register, a displacement, a protection flag and a length
> `[rcx+rdx*8+10h]` uses all of them: base `rcx`, index `rdx` scaled by 8, displacement `10h`.

? What is the difference between `movzx` and `movsx`?
+ Both widen; `movzx` fills with zeros, `movsx` with the sign bit
- `movzx` moves to memory, `movsx` moves to a register
- `movzx` clears the destination, `movsx` swaps the two operands
- `movzx` is for 32-bit values and `movsx` for 64-bit values
> So the byte `0xFE` becomes 254 with `movzx` and -2 with `movsx`.

? What does `lea` do?
- It loads the value stored at an address into a register
- It locks a memory location for one thread
+ It computes a memory operand's address without reading memory
- It loads the address of the next instruction
> Because it only computes, compilers also use it for fast arithmetic such as `lea eax, [rcx+rcx*2]` for `x * 3`.

? What does `mov eax, dword ptr [rcx+8]` do?
- Sets eax to rcx+8
+ Copies the 4 bytes at address rcx+8 into eax
- Adds 8 to the value at rcx
> The brackets read memory; `lea` would compute the address instead.

? The byte at `[rdx]` is `0xFE`. What does `movsx eax, byte ptr [rdx]` put in eax?
- 254
- 0xFE000000
+ -2
> Sign extension copies the top bit, so `0xFE` as a signed byte, -2, stays -2.

? Which C++ expression is `[rcx+rdx*8]` most likely to come from?
+ `p[i]` where `p` points at 8-byte values
- `p + i + 8` on a `char` pointer
- `p->member` at offset 8 of a struct
> Base, index and a scale equal to the element size: array indexing.

? Why might a compiler emit `lea eax, [rcx+rcx*2]`?
- To read memory at `x * 3`
+ To compute `x * 3` in one instruction
- To compare `x` with 3
> `lea` does arithmetic with the address hardware and never touches memory.
```
ideas:
- In the demonstration, change the scale from `*4` to `*8` and predict what goes wrong.
- Write `int f(int x) { return x * 9 + 3; }`, compile it with `cl /O2 /FA`, and find the `lea`.
- Look at a `->` access in Visual Studio's Disassembly window and match the displacement with the member's offset from `offsetof`.
